brief.head: Copycat capitalism
brief.text: Imported best practice made Indian firms more efficient but also more alike, Amit Varma warned, borrowing the biologists’ term isomorphic mimicry. {037-C04}

brief.head: Tastes on the move
brief.text: Tastes do not stay put, Amit Varma said: Tamils and Bengalis live all over India, so a firm could ship thirty flavours everywhere and let shopkeepers choose. {037-C13}

brief.head: Caps lock credit
brief.text: Lenders can judge your creditworthiness by whether you type in all caps, Amit Varma said, citing Rahul Matthan, or by how low you let your phone battery run. {037-S09}

brief.head: Stalin at HQ?
brief.text: Ronald Coase asked why firms run on central command inside while markets run on prices outside. Ajay Shah asks if the inside must be that Stalinist. {037-C10}

brief.head: Smaller than it looks
brief.text: India’s market is smaller than its 1.4 billion people, Amit Varma said, after Sajith Pai: for some products it may be just 20 lakh customers. {037-C11}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the Indian firm
lead.head: One firm, a hundred Indias
body: Amit Varma opened by promising to talk about “the boring subject of Bollywood”, while Ajay Shah took the Indian business landscape and the next 20 years. {037-J01}

It turned out to be one conversation. Varma’s first clip, a song from *Baazigar*, was read with mock gravity as a dissertation on why local knowledge beats bookish knowledge. That was Shah’s theme too.

His story of the Indian firm ran in three acts. In the first, firms were national only in name. In the second, technology made them truly national. In the third, still to come, they must learn to be local again.
## Out of headquarters’ reach
Until the 1980s, Shah said, a firm could operate all over India while its branch managers did their own thing. They had to be empowered, because they had no way to check back with headquarters.
That allowed sensible local adaptation, but also sloppy process and petty corruption. Shah borrowed Lant Pritchett’s image of the Indian state: a brain whose nerves to the fingers have been severed.
From the 1990s, computers and, above all, telecom ended that. For the first time, Indian firms had central information, central process design and operational controls. {037-C01}
Shah counts this as an engine of the GDP explosion from 1991 to 2011: firms grew in scale and productivity without adding much labour. Few people, he said, have remarked on it.
## The great flattening
Success brought its own trap. Firms came to believe in one firm, one list of products and one process design, rolled out all across India.
India is too diverse for that, Shah argued. He prefers the map drawn from CMIE’s household data: about 100 homogeneous regions, each a cluster of about seven districts within one state.
Measured that way, he said, India is more diverse than Europe or Africa. {037-C05}

Global firms already behave accordingly. Nestle tunes Maggi for each country. Why, Shah asked, should one Maggi, or one home-loan algorithm, serve all of India? “That really seems preposterous given the amount of diversity of India,” he said. {037-C06}
Varma pushed back: Amazon and YouTube already cater to a market of one. Shah replied that every personal prediction comes from a model fitted to a pool of people. The real decision is which pool.
## A treasury at the top

Shah’s prescription borrows from multinationals, which know Poland is different from France. Headquarters keeps strategy, capital, governance and the board. Regional units run their own profit and loss, adapt their products and models, and bid for capital. {037-C09}

“It is easy to be a simple Stalinist centralised firm rolling out everything all across the country,” he said. The adaptive firm is harder. But the national giants, for all their trillion-rupee valuations, have only scratched the surface of the Indian market.
Some, he expects, will learn to make their armour more flexible. The rest leave space for local firms.
Varma saw the shape of the whole: firms local because they had to be, then centralised by technology, coming full circle to local again.
He also had a compliment ready. India, he often says, inhabits three centuries at once. Shah’s mind, he added, is in the 22nd.

second.label: Taste of the market
second.head: Maggi with a passport
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why Maggi and Kit Kat taste different in every country
body: Buy Maggi noodles in Indonesia, India and the UK, Ajay Shah said, and you will find they all taste different. Nestle runs focus groups and research to find the right flavour for Thailand, Indonesia or India. {037-S04}

Kit Kat varies too. Fans revere the British original. Americans, Shah said, are stuck with a sugar-loaded version pushed by Hershey’s, and travellers to Japan carry bagfuls home. His advice: buy both in every country you visit. “It’s great fun.”

Then he turned the lesson on India. Would Tamilians and Punjabis eat the same Maggi? As India’s market approaches the size of an Indonesia or a Thailand, he argued, one product for the whole country stops making sense. {037-C06}

quote.text: The original British Kit Kat is perfect. Kit Kats in Japan are magical. Kit Kat in America are horrible.

second.caption: the Kit Kat test

third.head: The phone in her hand
body: For the decentralisation chapter of *In Service of the Republic*, his book with Vijay Kelkar, Ajay Shah lined up CMIE’s 100 homogeneous regions and compared the richest with the poorest. {037-S06}
The richest, he found, is about 5.3 times richer than the poorest. That was “a nice number to know”, he said, but not the one that stuck in his head.
The one that stuck was the share of women who own a mobile phone. It reflects a household’s prosperity, but also its social progressivity: whether it will give a teenage girl a phone at all.
In the top regions the share is about 18 times higher than in the bottom ones. “That’s huge levels of variation,” Shah said. {#eighteen}
third.caption: women and mobile phones

p2.title: The adaptive firm
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s case that Indian firms, having learnt to be national, must now learn to be local again

sections.label: The first age
sections.head: When the branch was a kingdom
sections.caption: the old Indian firm
body: In the bad old days, Ajay Shah said, you could build a firm that operated all over India, but its operational controls were very weak. Branch managers had to be empowered, because there was no way for them to check back with headquarters. {037-S01}

“I always like to remind everybody that Robert Clive did his own thing because there was no email,” he said. Indian branch managers were much the same: they had considerable discretion, and customers knew it was worth arguing with them. {037-S02}
Amit Varma saw a feature as well as a bug. Being in Patiala or in Patna makes a material difference to the approach you take with a customer, he said.
## A brain without nerves
The bug, Shah said, was process failure. Different people were idiosyncratic and did their own thing, and petty corruption crept in.

He borrowed Lant Pritchett’s description of the Indian state: a brain whose nerves have been severed, with the fingers doing their own thing. Every large firm became “a coalition of various individuals doing their own thing”, unable to hold to a strategy or manage risk. {037-C02}
Shah said he was not there to venerate that era, only to describe it. We have forgotten these things, he said, and think of them as prehistory.
~ Varma marked the moment with a clip from *Gangs of Wasseypur Part 2*, standing for headquarters’ disdain for a local manager who doesn’t get it. {037-J10}

quote.text: There is a brain, but the nerves have been severed and the fingers are doing their own thing.

sections.label: The second age
sections.head: Clive gets email
sections.caption: the true national firm
body: From the 1990s, Ajay Shah said, Indian firms got computers and, more importantly, telecom. Early VSAT links came in the late 1990s, and serious internet connectivity in the 2000s. {#vsat}

Firms now had centralised information, centralised process design and operational controls. Robert Clive was no longer a loose cannon far away. “Now Robert Clive was under the daily misery of surveillance from HQ,” Shah said. {037-C01}
## The engine nobody noticed

Shah counts this as one of the great developments of the Indian economy, a piece of the GDP explosion from 1991 to 2011. {#gdp} Andersen Consulting, now Accenture, helped spread process engineering and ERP systems across hundreds of firms, which grew in scale without adding much labour.

Until then, he said, telecom had been the choke point, either unavailable or priced “outright crazy”. In the Vajpayee years, Sudheendra Kulkarni and N.K. Singh “did amazing things” and blew up the Department of Telecom’s “death grip”. {037-J13}

Amit Varma wondered how much came from imported ideas, with the danger of isomorphic mimicry. Shah said the channel was less the business schools than the practices of global firms: in banking, through foreign banks and people who had worked in them. {037-C04}
~ Shah admires that work. But, he warned, it came with a difficulty of its own.

quote.text: This is the heart, the engine of how sophisticated scale and productivity emerged in Indian capitalism.

sections.label: The catch
sections.head: More diverse than a continent
sections.caption: India’s hundred regions
body: The difficulty, Ajay Shah said, was excessive centralisation. Firms got “drugged” on the idea of one firm, one list of products and one process design, rolled out across all of India, flattening the country’s richness and complexity.

His alternative map comes from CMIE’s household data, which divides India into about 100 homogeneous regions. Each is a contiguous group of districts within one state, with similar women’s literacy and a similar agroclimatic zone. After more than 10 years, he is “a great enthusiast”. {037-R12}
With India at 140 crore people, that is about 14 million people per region, or seven districts on average. {#fourteen}
## Borders by accident
Nor should a firm think in states. “Like really should UP be one state? Okay, it makes no sense,” Shah said. {037-J05}

Measured region by region, India is more diverse than Europe or Africa, he argued. Lant Pritchett once told him that by some measures India’s gap between top and bottom is wider than that of Latin America and Africa merged, which would mean reversing geological drift. {037-C05}
~ So why, Shah asked, should a lender’s software use the identical home-loan algorithm in every corner of the country? {037-C06}

quote.text: Don’t even think of India as a bunch of states because the state boundaries are kinda random.

sections.label: The pushback
sections.head: A data set of one won’t do
sections.caption: the market of one
body: Amit Varma was not convinced by the 100 regions. With 1.4 billion Indians, he said, there are in a sense 1.4 billion homogeneous regions, and technology already caters to each. His Amazon algorithm does not show him what it shows somebody else in Mumbai.
Ajay Shah replied that the underlying code could still differ by country. Somebody is estimating a model, and that model can work at different levels of abstraction.
## The pooling question

His example was the credit card default prediction model, “the engine inside every financial firm that issues a credit card”. {#creditcard} A prediction for one customer still needs data pooled across many. {037-C07} Which pool, the world, India, South India, Tamil Nadu or one region, is “the decision box”.
If farmers kill themselves in Marathwada, Shah said, that shapes his thinking about the model for Marathwada differently. {#marathwada}
Varma brought in Rahul Matthan’s *The Third Way*: lenders now judge creditworthiness by whether you type in all caps, or whether you let your phone battery run down to 3 or 4 per cent. {037-S09}
~ Varma conceded the point for the real world. Nestle, he said, cannot make 1.4 billion Maggi flavours, even if his YouTube feed is his alone.

quote.text: You can’t make a prediction for a customer of one with a data set of one.

sections.label: The fix
sections.head: Poland is not France
sections.caption: the federated firm
body: How should a firm redesign itself to serve many Indias? The answers, Ajay Shah said, are “actually not that hard”: imagine you were a company operating in 20 countries.

Every global corporation knows that Poland is different from France, he said. {#poland} Their offerings combine the central and the local: some things are done differently for Poland, some differently for France. Indian firms can borrow that knowledge and doctrine.
## A federation of mini CEOs

The core would be a headquarters for strategy, capital allocation, governance, the board and HR. Around it would sit a federated, decentralised architecture of business groups, each in charge of its own profit and loss. The one sent to conquer UP and Bihar would be “like a mini CEO”, with considerable freedom.
Later he sharpened the idea. Headquarters would be the treasury, and regional units would bid for its capital, competing with one another on return on equity. {037-C09}

Firms can sit anywhere on a spectrum. At one end is Casio, which says, in Shah’s caricature: “This is my watch, hell with you, I’m just selling this watch.” Only its advertising and distribution change. {#casio}
~ At the other end, product, process and service grow ever more flexible. Those are the trade-offs, Shah said, that managers will need to address in India in coming years.

quote.text: The various sub firms all over India should be in an auction where they ask for capital and then they use it efficiently.

sections.label: The rethink
sections.head: Seeing like a firm
sections.caption: the blind national firm
body: Amit Varma asked how much large firms could mimic the bottom-up processes that work so well in society.

Ajay Shah began with Ronald Coase, who first asked why firms run on central command inside while the world outside runs on contracts and prices. Today, Shah said, we can ask: “Do you really need to be that Stalinist?” {037-C10}
## The blind giant

James C Scott’s *Seeing Like a State* describes states unable to perceive ground reality. Big national firms, Shah argued, share the blindness. They serve one slice of the income distribution in each region and leave large parts of the country unserved. {037-C08}
That leaves room for local firms, like the deeply optimised Rajasthan firm, even though nobody can match the national firms’ cost of capital.
His test is to compute revenue, profit or return on equity in each homogeneous region. If the numbers are widely dispersed, he said, “to some extent I’ll turn around and blame the firm.” {037-C12}
Serving the weakest regions, where people have some disposable income too, means getting off the high horse of one product for all India.
~ The case grows with the market. In 1991, Shah recalled, all of Bank of America’s Indian operations were like those in some small American state. {037-S07}

quote.text: But the arrogance of the big national firm makes it blind. It makes it difficult for the firm to see that reality.

side.boxText: Ronald Coase’s *The Nature of the Firm* asked why firms are run centrally inside while markets outside run on contracts and prices. Ajay Shah took it as his starting point for asking whether firms need so much central control inside. {037-C10}

contQuote.text: All of us have lived it, we’ve just stopped noticing it, and I want to pull this out of our consciousness and say that this was big, this was huge.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: From an airline counter to Nehru’s jail, four tales and their lessons

stories.start: And in my mind, the single vision that I want you to think about
stories.end: and also engaged in their own petty biases and local corruption
stories.caption: the Indian Airlines employee
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on where power sat in the old Indian firm
stories.head: The demigod behind the desk
body: Picture a customer, in the days before the 1990s, arguing with an Indian Airlines frontline employee: earnestly, sincerely, pleading, “Do something for me.” For Ajay Shah, that scene sums up the old Indian firm. {037-S02}
The customer was not wasting breath. “Actually, the frontline employees of Indian Airlines had a lot of discretion,” Shah said. “They could do many things. They were seriously powerful people.”

Banks worked the same way. The teller was reasonably disempowered. But the branch manager “was like a demigod”, with serious discretion over genuinely important decisions, and that made it worth your while arguing with him.

The reason was technology. A firm could operate all over India, but with no way for managers to check back with headquarters, they had to be empowered. Robert Clive, as Shah likes to remind everybody, did his own thing because there was no email. {037-S01}
So power sat at the local front line. Staff thought for themselves and evolved the offering in ways that made sense, and also indulged their own petty biases and local corruption.
Computers and telecom would later drain that discretion away to headquarters.

~ Amit Varma heard in this the answer to a puzzle. Working at a Starbucks, he had overheard a woman lose her temper with Amazon customer care and vow never to buy from the company again. The agent was a call-centre worker with a script, who could not help her. “But this kind of explains why that habit would have been there,” Varma said. {037-S03}
stories.why: Whom customers bother to persuade shows where power sits in an organisation. And habits outlive the design that formed them: people still argue with frontline staff who no longer have any discretion.

stories.start: So I want to give you one simple example. Kerala turns out.
stories.end: that North Kerala is different from Central Kerala, is different from South Kerala
stories.caption: the three Keralas
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on CMIE’s map of a southern state
stories.head: Kerala in three, not ten
body: CMIE’s algorithm groups India’s roughly 700 districts into about 100 homogeneous regions. {#districts} Ajay Shah’s simple example is Kerala, which comes out as three. {037-S05}
“There’s North Kerala, there’s central Kerala, and there’s South Kerala,” he said.

He has discussed the finding with many people who know the state, and their verdict was: this makes sense. Kerala is actually quite diverse. The north differs from the middle, and the middle from the south, in interesting and important ways.
~ Just as important, three is the right level of abstraction. You do not want to go to ten. A good map, in Shah’s telling, is fine enough to show real differences and simple enough to stay useful.

quote.text: Kerala is about three pieces and you should think about them differently.

stories.start: So, for example, I know some firms who really are in their comfort zone
stories.end: and mutter wake curses at the difficulties of operating in the
stories.caption: firms that shun the North
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on firms that will not go north
stories.head: Mutter curses, miss markets
body: Ajay Shah knows some firms that are in their comfort zone playing South India. Ask them about the North and they will mutter strange curses. {037-S08}
North India, they say, is some wasteland: they don’t know how to operate there, and they won’t. You could behave like that, Shah said.

His advice is to hire some “red-blooded North Indians” and figure out how to play in that market, because there is some upside there. The tidy, calm ways of operating in the south won’t work there, he said. Working out what will is the firm’s job.
~ Amit Varma objected to the phrase. “Everyone is red-blooded,” he said. “I did not expect the sad stereotyping from you.” {037-J06}
stories.why: When a firm calls a market too difficult, Shah suggested, it is often describing the limits of its own understanding. A wide gap in profits between regions points to a failure of the firm, not the market. {037-C12}

stories.start: And is it true? I mean, I vaguely seem to remember, I don't know
stories.end: glimpses of world history is his letters to Iner Gandhi is just done from
stories.caption: Nehru’s prison desk
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the book he understood only as an adult
stories.head: History, from memory
body: Ajay Shah’s recommendation was a book most Indians meet in childhood: Jawaharlal Nehru’s *The Discovery of India*. He read it at 12 or so, and woke up to it only slowly. {#twelve}
Rereading it as a grown-up a couple of years ago, he found it “literally the book that invents the idea of India”. {037-R07}

Amit Varma asked whether Nehru had written it in prison, with the quotes and references from memory. He was in jail, Shah said, but political prisoners were treated well and he was given access to books. He had no library and no computer, only a couple of books on his desk that friends rotated. {037-S10}
~ *Glimpses of World History*, his letters to Indira Gandhi, was also done from memory. Varma’s verdict: “He would have been a podcaster today.” {037-J09}
stories.why: These founding books came out of what one mind could hold. Shah urges adults who read *The Discovery of India* as children to go back to it; Varma urges children to read it now.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, did Robert Clive get to do his own thing?
quiz.a: Because there was no email: headquarters had no way to check on him.

quiz.q: Why was it rational to argue with an Indian Airlines frontline employee in the old days?
quiz.a: Those employees had real discretion; Shah calls them seriously powerful people.

quiz.q: How many homogeneous regions does Kerala split into on CMIE’s map, and what are they?
quiz.a: Three: North, central and South Kerala; Shah says three, not ten, is right.

quiz.q: Which single statistic about women stayed in Ajay Shah’s head from the regional data?
quiz.a: The share of women owning a mobile phone, about 18 times higher at the top.

quiz.q: Which credit-scoring signals did Amit Varma cite from his conversation with Rahul Matthan?
quiz.a: Whether you type in all caps, and how low you let your phone battery run.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s federated firm, what role does headquarters play for the regional units?
quiz.a: It acts as treasury; regions bid for capital and compete on return on equity.
